summary: This Experimental document optimizes BFD Authentication so it scales better. It splits authentication into a more computationally intensive mechanism applied to significant packets and a lighter mechanism for the rest, so not every control packet pays the full cost.

eli5.summary: A guard checks ID closely at the door for important visitors, but only glances at the regular ones to save time.

questions: what is mci and lci authentication in bfd
how often does bfd reauthenticate with mci
subtitle: Spend heavy authentication only on the BFD packets that change something, and use a lighter check for the steady stream of Up packets.

tldr.problem: BFD authenticates every control packet the same way, and because BFD sends packets at a high rate on often resource-constrained devices, that cost discourages operators from turning authentication on.
tldr.mechanism: Authentication is split into a more computationally intensive (MCI) mechanism for packets that signal significant changes and a less computationally intensive (LCI) mechanism for the rest. A periodic Poll sequence authenticated with MCI re-tests the session, and one Auth Type value signals the pairing.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is Experimental. It says there are no known implementations and that implementations based on it should not be considered compliant with BFD.

today: RFC 9985, published in June 2026, is an Experimental RFC and not part of the Standards Track, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its appendix says there are no known implementations at this time and that the work could become valuable if deploying BFD Authentication at scale becomes a reality.

sections.title: The Cost of Authenticating Every Packet
sections.content:
BFD (RFC 5880) authenticates each control packet with the same mechanism when authentication is enabled. Devices running BFD are often resource-constrained. In software, authentication competes with other work, and hardware acceleration still imposes a cost. BFD's value depends on handling many sessions and sending control packets at a high rate, so implementers and operators must weigh the benefit of authentication against its impact on performance.

The mechanisms in RFC 5880, MD5 and SHA-1, are described as not particularly strong in a cryptographic sense, yet may still not scale in a given implementation. Stronger mechanisms in the future would likely use even more resources.

The RFC's key observation is that the packets needed to signal state changes are very few, while the great majority just confirm that the session remains Up. It partitions authentication to match.
sections.eli5: Checking every visitor's ID very carefully makes the line at the door crawl. Most visitors are just the same regulars again and again, so the guard saves the careful check for the moments that matter.

sections.title: Significant Changes, MCI and LCI
sections.content:
A significant change is a state change, a demand mode change (the D bit), or a poll sequence change (the P or F bit). Changes to control packet contents that do not need a poll sequence, such as bfd.DetectMult, also count. The authentication applied to these packets is MCI (more computationally intensive), and the mechanism for all other packets is LCI (less computationally intensive). The RFC avoids calling them strong and weak so as not to imply a statement about cryptographic strength.

Every control packet in the AdminDown, Down or Init states MUST use MCI authentication. After the session reaches Up, it keeps using MCI for a period, then MAY switch to LCI. The contents of an Up packet must not change, aside from the Authentication Section, unless MCI authentication is in use.

The only LCI Auth Type named so far is Meticulous Keyed ISAAC from RFC 9986. It protects Up packets that do not change because only the paired devices know the shared secret, key and sequence number needed to select the ISAAC result. Other mechanisms may be defined later.
sections.eli5: Big moments, like starting or stopping the game, get the careful ID check. The ordinary "still here" waves only need the quick check.

sections.title: The Optimized Authentication Section
sections.content:
A single Auth Type value signals a pairing of an MCI type and an LCI type. That tells implementations that optimized procedures are in use, which pairing applies, that a Sequence Number is required and that the current mode is carried in the packet. The common section holds Auth Type, Auth Len, Auth Key ID, an Optimized Authentication Mode byte, a 32-bit Sequence Number and then Authentication Specific Data. The Auth Type and Auth Len values come from the companion documents for each pairing.

The Mode field is 1 for the MCI type and 2 for the LCI type. When the MCI type is used, the rest of the section carries that type's data.

A received packet MUST be discarded in these cases:

  • It has no Authentication Section or an unsupported Auth Type.
  • The Mode field is not 1 or 2.
  • The session state is AdminDown, Down or Init and the Mode is not 1.
  • The session is Up, the packet is a significant change and the Mode is not 1.
  • Auth Len does not fit the Mode.
  • The sequence number is outside the range from bfd.RcvAuthSeq+1 to bfd.RcvAuthSeq+(3*Detect Mult), when bfd.AuthSeqKnown is 1.

Otherwise the receiver runs the authentication procedure for the Auth Type and Mode, and accepts the packet only if it succeeds.
sections.eli5: Each wave carries a small badge that says which kind of check it needs: careful or quick. The listener refuses any wave whose badge does not fit the moment.

sections.title: Switching Modes and Reauthenticating
sections.content:
MCI authentication brings a session to Up and carries any parameter change. After the session is Up, the Up state MUST be signaled with MCI for at least the Detection Time before switching to LCI, which lets ISAAC or another light mechanism be bootstrapped. The RFC recommends switching after at least that interval, so that if LCI is broken the remote system can tear the session down quickly. A session that reaches Up with MCI but fails with LCI SHOULD be brought to the operator's attention, and implementations MAY throttle session restarts. It also recommends delaying the Up notification to the client until LCI is working.

While LCI is in use, BFD should periodically test the session with MCI by starting a Poll sequence authenticated with MCI. If no packet with the Final (F) bit arrives using MCI within twice the Detect Interval as the receiving system would calculate it, the session is considered compromised and MUST be brought down. The interval for these tests is configurable. The RFC gives every one minute as an example of how a small share of Up packets can cut the computational load while keeping the session secure over that interval.

This does not change the BFD state machine. A packet that fails authentication, or should have been MCI-authenticated but was not, is simply discarded.
sections.eli5: Every so often the guard asks a regular to show the full ID again. If they cannot answer in time, the guard sends them away.

sections.title: The Optimized Auth YANG Module
sections.content:
The ietf-bfd-opt-auth module augments the authentication container of the BFD YANG model (RFC 9314) for single-hop, multihop, LAG and MPLS sessions. It adds one leaf, reauth-interval, a uint32 in seconds with a default of 60. A value of zero means no periodic reauthentication with MCI, and the value SHOULD have jitter applied so sessions do not synchronize their expensive operations.

Operators enable the optimization by choosing one of the key-chain crypto-algorithms defined by the ietf-bfd-met-keyed-isaac module in RFC 9986. The appendix shows a single-hop session with a reauth interval of 30 seconds.
sections.eli5: It is one setting that says how often the guard should ask for the full ID again.

sections.title: Security Trade-offs
sections.content:
The MCI mechanism is expected to have cryptographic strength acceptable for authenticating a whole BFD session as described in RFC 5880. It protects against improperly starting sessions and against changing session parameters or resetting a session. In the Up state, LCI resists keeping a session Up inappropriately. Because state changes need MCI and Up-packet contents must stay unchanged, successful spoofing of LCI packets can only keep a session Up. Periodic MCI reauthentication protects against long-term successful spoofing of LCI.

The goal is therefore to make it hard to reset or wrongly start sessions, while accepting that keeping a session Up is a less interesting attack that can receive less protection. Operators must weigh the trade-off. The RFC also says the attacks on MD5 and SHA-1 raise concerns, and that stronger algorithms would make authenticating every packet even harder.

For the YANG module, reauth-interval is sensitive. Set very low, it lessens the benefit. Set very high, attacks found by MCI may be detected late. Out-of-band keys must be well chosen and protected.
sections.eli5: A trickster can only make the guard keep a door open a bit longer, not open new doors or close them, and the regular full checks catch even that after a while.
